    Swiss franc floor, 2011–15ECB bond backstop, 2012

    Switzerland · 2011–2015

    The franc floor and the rate cut

    On 15 January 2015 the Swiss National Bank removed the franc’s floor against the euro and cut interest rates. The two decisions worked in different directions. Reading the rate line alone gives an incomplete account of the change in borrowing and trading conditions.

    1. 6 Sep 2011

      A minimum price for the euro

      The SNB committed to buying foreign currency in unlimited quantities if one euro threatened to buy less than CHF 1.20. This put a ceiling on the franc’s strength against the euro. A rate-series observer saw no step that day. The commitment changed the price at which the central bank stood ready to trade.

      Minimum exchange rate decision
    2. 18 Dec 2014

      A charge on eligible franc balances

      The SNB retained the floor and announced a −0.25% charge on sight deposits above an exemption threshold, originally scheduled to start on 22 January. It widened its three-month Libor target range to −0.75% to +0.25%. Its midpoint dropped from +0.125% to −0.25%. The chart records that December move even though the deposit charge had yet to take effect.

      Decision and deposit terms
    3. 15 Jan 2015

      The floor ends and the rate falls again

      The bank ended the CHF 1.20 commitment immediately and shifted the Libor range to −1.25% to −0.25%. The midpoint fell another 50 basis points. It also set the sight-deposit charge at −0.75% for 22 January. Lower remuneration discouraged demand for francs while ending the floor allowed them to appreciate.

      Discontinuation and new target range

    What changed outside the rate series?

    The SNB’s 2014 annual report records CHF 25.8 billion of foreign-currency purchases late that year. The 2015 report records CHF 86.1 billion across the full year, mostly in January. That total includes purchases on both sides of the regime change. Treating it all as the cost of defending the floor would overstate what the figure measures.

    2014 annual report · 2015 annual report

    What would distinguish the explanations?

    A falling rate could be read as an independent response to a weakening domestic outlook. The joint announcement also supports an exchange-rate explanation. In April, the SNB said prolonged euro weakness would have required interventions of rapidly increasing size. Comparing franc rates and euro cross-rates with inflation expectations and Swiss credit terms would help separate the external pressure from domestic transmission. Two instruments changed together, so their separate effects cannot be recovered from this decision alone.

    SNB’s April retrospective · BIS instrument definition, p. 10

    Who faced the new interest rate?

    The SNB charged eligible sight-deposit balances above their exemption thresholds. To test how much of the charge reached households or firms, compare deposit and lending rates at banks with different amounts of exposed balances before and after 22 January.

    Euro area · July–September 2012

    A bond backstop without a purchase

    The ECB’s main refinancing rate stayed at 0.75% from 25 July to 10 September. During that interval the prospect of a conditional buyer changed what investors could expect if a sovereign bond sell-off threatened the transmission of monetary policy. Three announcements tell different parts of the story.

    1. 26 Jul 2012

      A commitment to preserve the euro

      In London, Mario Draghi distinguished the risk that debt could be repaid in a different currency from default and liquidity risk. He argued that a premium linked to the euro’s convertibility could obstruct common monetary policy. His speech signalled a willingness to act within the ECB’s mandate. It specified neither a purchase schedule nor which bonds could qualify.

      London remarks
    2. 2 Aug 2012

      The Council describes a possible instrument

      The Governing Council said it could undertake outright operations to restore transmission. Governments would need to fulfil their commitments and seek the appropriate assistance through the euro-area rescue funds. Draghi explained that such action was a necessary precondition and the ECB would still decide independently whether to intervene. Design work continued.

      Council statement and questions
    3. 6 Sep 2012

      The purchase rules become public

      Outright Monetary Transactions could buy sovereign bonds on secondary markets, concentrating on maturities of one to three years. The ECB required an appropriate EFSF or ESM programme with enforceable conditions and retained discretion to start, suspend or stop purchases. It set no advance numerical limit, intended equal creditor treatment and would absorb the liquidity created. Existing Securities Markets Programme holdings remained on a separate book.

      OMT technical features

    What changed in the market’s downside scenario?

    By June 2019, Draghi reported that OMT had never been activated. The programme therefore made no purchases in the 2012 episode. He also reported that spreads in vulnerable countries fell by more than 400 basis points on average over the next two years. That horizon includes subsequent policy decisions and economic news. It cannot measure the impact of any single announcement.

    ECB retrospective, June 2019 · July rate decision and settlement date

    Was it currency risk, credit risk or liquidity?

    Compare short sovereign spreads over euro overnight swaps around each announcement with longer maturities, fiscal news and bond bid–ask spreads. One ECB working paper also compares the cost of insuring the same sovereign in dollars and euros, relative to Germany, to isolate exposure to repayment in another currency. Falling currency-sensitive premiums alongside narrower cross-border bank funding spreads would support the transmission explanation. Simultaneous rescue-fund news, collateral changes and shifting default risk can also move bond prices. Spreads on their own cannot separate those effects.

    Redenomination measure, Working Paper 1785 · Other September measures
